video_title: Norman Finkelstein: Can Anyone STOP Israel? | October 7, Three Years Later
gist: Three years after October 7, Norman Finkelstein argues that US opinion has flipped on Gaza (30-40% of American Jews say genocide) while campuses capitulated to donor pressure, and that Israeli polling shows Netanyahu is a symptom of society rather than the cause. On Iran, he says the ceasefire holds because Trump has no war option, Hormuz has reached a modus vivendi, no Trump-Iran deal is possible, and China is the main winner as Iran becomes dependent on it.

insights.claim: Before October 7, 2023 a pro-Gaza plank would sink a US political campaign; three years later it lifts campaigns at local, senatorial and gubernatorial levels.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Israel policy has flipped from electoral liability to asset for some candidates, shifting the odds on future US aid and arms-transfer politics.
insights.quote: A plank in support of Gaza, not only doesn't sink the ship, it boys the ship, it lifts it.

insights.claim: Recent polls show 30-40% of American Jews believe Israel committed genocide in Gaza, which Finkelstein calls unpredictable given lifelong pro-Israel socialization.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Erosion of support in a core pro-Israel constituency weakens the domestic coalition behind unconditional US support.
insights.quote: The most recent polls show that between 30 and 40% of American Jews believe that Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza.

insights.claim: Public opinion shifted over about a year and a half because social and web media out-competed legacy outlets like the New York Times, which by year two were 'playing catchup with reality'.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Narrative power has moved from legacy media to platforms; legacy outlets' framing now lags opinion rather than leading it.
insights.quote: the legacy media was playing catchup with reality

insights.claim: The main driver of the opinion shift was that Israel's conduct was openly visible in real time, with soldiers posting their actions on social media rather than concealing them.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Real-time, unconcealable footage changes how conflicts are priced politically; reputational costs build faster.
insights.quote: they carried it out in broad daylight in real time

insights.claim: Young people's solidarity with Gaza partly reflects their own economic precarity: gig work, close to zero prospect of homeownership or family formation, and atomization without big factory workplaces to build collective power.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Youth economic distress is a political accelerant that could feed anti-establishment voting and labor or housing politics beyond foreign policy.
insights.quote: The prospect of owning a home is zero. the prospect of raising a family close to zero.

insights.claim: A rally for Brad Landler, a self-described Jewish Zionist and confidant of Zohran Mamdani running in a heavily Jewish district, was entirely about Gaza and Jewish-Muslim unity.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Even in Jewish-heavy districts, Gaza solidarity has become a mainstream campaign theme.

insights.claim: Opposition to Israeli policy is growing among younger Republicans, and figures like Candace Owens, Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene are trying to capitalize on it.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: A bipartisan generational split on Israel raises long-run risk to the consensus behind US military aid.

insights.claim: The Democratic Party is 'rapidly getting a facelift' on Israel, and the UK's new Burnham government with Foreign Secretary Miliband is moving in a positive direction.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Western governments may tighten arms-export and diplomatic policy toward Israel, a policy risk for Israeli defense trade.

insights.claim: Popular pressure from below is the force most able to constrain Israel outside Israel itself, and must be kept on politicians like Mamdani, whose handling of Netanyahu's UN visit disappointed Finkelstein.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Activist pressure on newly elected progressives is a live variable in local and national policy.

insights.claim: Universities, hospitals and cultural institutions capitulated on free speech about Gaza even as Gaza gained positive salience in electoral politics, two contradictory trends at once.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Institutional risk aversion under donor and political pressure is a governance signal for higher education and nonprofits.
insights.quote: in universities, hospitals, cultural institutions, there's a veritable reign of terror

insights.claim: Billionaire donors such as Bill Ackman at Harvard ($50M given) and Robert Kraft at Columbia pressured universities, but with endowments like Harvard's $50 billion the institutions could have withstood the withdrawal of gifts.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Donor leverage over elite universities is out of proportion to the money involved; endowment size does not shield governance.
insights.quote: they had very large endowments in the Harvard $50 billion

insights.claim: An Amnesty International and ACLU report documents campus repression, including worse police brutality and discipline at CUNY than at Columbia, with CUNY getting far less coverage because its students are mostly poor, Black and brown.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Media coverage tracks institutional prestige, not severity, so the press undercounts risk at non-elite institutions.

insights.claim: Columbia president Minouche Shafik called in police and imposed punitive measures, yet was removed anyway; capitulation did not protect her.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Leaders who give in to pressure campaigns may still lose their jobs, so capitulation is a poor survival strategy.

insights.claim: The leading scholarly authority on Gaza has received no invitations from roughly 60 nearby New York colleges, and his book Gaza's Gravediggers got no reviews, evidence the gatekeeping system works.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Gatekeeping by academia and publishing suppresses dissenting expertise, so mainstream consensus may lag the evidence.
insights.quote: The current book's gravediggers. Certainly my um salience has been significant since October 7th. Not one review.

insights.claim: The Biden administration, not Trump, presided over the encampment crackdowns and supplied about 70% of the weapons used in Gaza, a fact the Amnesty/ACLU report omits.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: US arms supply is the key enabler on both sides of the aisle; framing that blames only Trump is incomplete.
insights.quote: Do you know 70% of the weapons came from the US?

themes.theme: Israeli public opinion and Netanyahu's durability

insights.claim: Netanyahu is not the cause but the effect: he keeps winning because he mirrors Israeli society, so the Atlantic/New York Times narrative that removing him fixes Israel is wrong.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Don't expect a change of leader to change Israeli policy much; regime-change trades on Netanyahu's exit are mispriced.
insights.quote: He's not the problem. He's the effect. The cause is Israel, the people.

insights.claim: Polls predicting Netanyahu's exit appear every six months and keep failing; he remains Israel's longest-serving prime minister.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Fade the recurring 'Netanyahu is finished' headlines.

insights.claim: Israeli polling has been steady: about 5% of Israeli Jews say Israel uses too much force in Gaza, about 55% say the right amount and about 40% too little.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Domestic Israeli consensus offers no internal brake on military escalation.
insights.quote: 5% of Israeli Jews said too much force.

insights.claim: A poll found 47% of Israeli Jews said soldiers entering a Gaza city should kill everyone, and 62% of all Israelis (about 70-75% of Jews) said there are no innocents in Gaza.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Hardline public opinion locks in policy regardless of who governs.
insights.quote: 47% of Israeli Jews said yes.

insights.claim: In July 2025, between the full March-May blockade and the IPC's August famine finding, 79% of Israeli Jews said they were not at all or only a little concerned about reports of starvation in Gaza.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Humanitarian pressure gets little traction inside Israel; any constraint must come from outside.
insights.quote: Do you know what 79% of Israeli Jews said? Not at all or just a little bit.

insights.claim: Israeli ignorance of Gaza conditions is not credible as an excuse, because Israel has the highest per-capita web use in the world.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Opinion reflects preference, not lack of information, so information campaigns are unlikely to move Israeli policy.
insights.quote: Israel has the highest per capita usage of the web of any country in the world.

insights.claim: Because the IDF is a citizen army that cross-sections society, with no meaningful anti-war movement, its conduct is representative of Israel, unlike US troops in Vietnam.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: There is no domestic anti-war constituency to force a change in policy.

insights.claim: At the UN, Netanyahu boasted of fighting on six fronts (Gaza, West Bank, Syria, Iraq, Yemen and others) and attacked Turkey, signaling Turkey may be the next front.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Israel-Turkey friction is a regional escalation risk worth watching.
insights.quote: And then he starts attacking Turkey. So we know Turkeykey's next.

themes.theme: October 7 intelligence and Israel's war aims

insights.claim: The Atlantic's reports of Egyptian warnings before October 7 do not show Netanyahu knew or wanted the attack: states get thousands of threat reports daily, and racist dismissal of Arab sources explains why the warnings were ignored.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Discount 'let it happen' narratives; they serve an elite effort to remove Netanyahu.

insights.claim: Hamas's attack was likely a last-minute decision, possibly triggered after Egypt learned of the plot and told Israel; fighters got orders at 2-3am and some showed up in pajamas, and Iran and Hezbollah were probably not told.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Supports the view that October 7 was not an Iran-coordinated axis operation, which bears on escalation logic.
insights.quote: a lot of people showed up in their pajamas for the attack

insights.claim: The Mossad is backed by Western and Arab intelligence services (German, French, UK, US, Egyptian, Jordanian, Qatari, Saudi, Bahraini), just as Russia is really fighting NATO rather than Ukraine alone.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Assess Israel's intelligence and military reach as a coalition capability, not a single-state one.

insights.claim: Israel's post-October 7 goals were to restore deterrence (Arab fear of Israel), take revenge, and turn the crisis into an opportunity to settle the Gaza, West Bank, Hezbollah and Iran 'questions'.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: A sequential strategic agenda implies the West Bank escalation continues and the risk stays across several fronts.

insights.claim: Hezbollah lost its independence after Nasrallah's death and has become a pawn of Iran.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Lebanon front risk now tracks Tehran's decisions more directly.

insights.claim: Of about 1,200 Israelis killed on October 7, about 850 were civilians, and Finkelstein sees no reason to doubt the numbers.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: A baseline casualty figure that anchors the deterrence and revenge motives.
insights.quote: 1,200 people were killed. Of those 1,200, about 850 were civilians.

themes.theme: Iran war, Hormuz and China as winner

insights.claim: Iran proved a far more formidable foe than Israel expected; withstanding the US and Israel despite sanctions since 1979 may be a turning point, and Israel did not achieve its Iran goal.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Reassess Iran's staying power; regime-collapse scenarios look less likely.
insights.quote: the Iranians proved to be a much more formidable foe than the Israelis in their uber mention mentality could have conceived

insights.claim: Finkelstein says he alone called that the US-Iran ceasefire would hold because Trump has no war option, predicting flare-ups but no resumption of full-scale war.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: A base case of a frozen conflict with skirmishes, not renewed full war, which limits oil tail risk.
insights.quote: He doesn't have a war option.

insights.claim: A modus vivendi has formed in the Strait of Hormuz: enough ships now pass that it is no longer a crisis, though the world economy suffered from the double blockade.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Shipping and oil-flow normalization through Hormuz reduces the energy-shock premium.
insights.quote: enough ships are passing at this point that it's not posing a crisis anymore

insights.claim: Predicted July and August economic crashes driven by the Hormuz oil disruption did not happen; the economy is surviving, though not thriving.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Markets may have overpriced recession risk from the Gulf disruption; resilience is the observed outcome.
insights.quote: they were predicting a crash in July in the economy because of the oil problem

insights.claim: There is zero chance of a Trump-Iran agreement, since neither side will accept the other's terms; Iran will wait out Trump's remaining two years and the issue will pass to the next president.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Expect sanctions and an unresolved standoff to persist through Trump's term, with no deal-driven return of Iranian barrels.
insights.quote: there is no possibility, none whatsoever, zero, that Trump will sign an agreement with Iran

insights.claim: China is the main beneficiary: it sustains Iran's economy, the US gets a 'good beating' that deters attacks on China, and Iran, the most formidable power in the Middle East, becomes wholly dependent on Beijing.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Watch China-Iran oil and trade ties deepen, a structural shift in Gulf energy flows and influence away from the US.
insights.quote: Iran becomes totally dependent on China. That's a gift that was handed to China.

insights.claim: Trump's prediction that Iranians would rise up failed: secular Iranian expatriates who hate the mullahs backed Iran during the war, and an estimated 40 million of 90 million Iranians attended Khamenei's funeral.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Rally-around-the-flag effects make regime change a weak investment thesis.
insights.quote: the population of Iran is 90 million. The estimate 40 million people were in the streets.

insights.claim: Ancient civilizations like China and Iran take a long view; China is patient because it believes the world's center of gravity is moving its way.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Expect patient, attrition-based strategies from Beijing and Tehran rather than rushed concessions.
insights.quote: the Chinese know the center of gravity in the world is moving in their direction

themes.theme: Trump presidency and US electoral dynamics

insights.claim: Trump is unprecedented in that national interest is only background music; his priorities are vanity and pageantry, and money and deals.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Model US policy as transactional and spectacle-driven: deals and personal wins outrank strategic coherence.
insights.quote: In the forefront of his mind, he has only two sets of concerns. Number one, van vanity and pageantry. Number two, money and deals.

insights.claim: Trump will never admit he lost the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Expect face-saving framing rather than policy reversal, which prolongs the standoff.
insights.quote: Trump will simply not admit he lost the war.

insights.claim: Trump's power comes less from media savvy than from an opposition of elitist 'woke liberals' who look down on his base; an authentic working-class candidate like Bernie Sanders would have beaten him.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Populist authenticity, not ideology, is the swing variable in US elections, which matters for 2028 policy scenarios.
insights.quote: Bernie Sanders would have shredded Trump.

insights.claim: Given a choice between being woke and being rich, the Democratic establishment chooses rich, as when it backed Andrew Cuomo over Zohran Mamdani.
insights.speaker: Norman Finkelstein
insights.so_what: Establishment-versus-insurgent fights inside the Democratic Party will shape the policy mix.
insights.quote: If it's a choice between being woke and being rich, they'll choose rich.

insights.claim: Robinson Erhardt argues that Trump's media mastery is real and intuitive, like Messi with soccer, and that moves such as banning CNN are deliberate distractions.
insights.speaker: Robinson Erhardt
insights.so_what: Treat headline-grabbing media fights as possible cover for bigger policy moves.
